Memorandum from the Theatre Scheduling Office, Halvering General Hospital, to the surgical directorate. Subject: whether the elective list for Thursday 3 September can stand as booked.

The Elective Admissions Standard, section 4, sets the baseline: no elective procedure under general anaesthesia may be listed unless the patient has attended a pre-operative anaesthetic assessment within the thirty days before the date of surgery. The standard describes this as a hard stop; the scheduling system rejects a booking whose assessment date falls outside the window, and the coordinator must re-book the assessment rather than the surgery. Section 4 applies to all surgical specialties on the Halvering and Cotterell sites.

Section 4.3 carves out patients who are under continuous care of a named consultant anaesthetist for a series of related procedures, for example staged reconstructions. For those patients the assessment done before the first procedure in the series carries forward, provided the anaesthetist has reviewed the notes and countersigned the list. Section 9, the definitions section, states that "continuous care" means the same named consultant anaesthetist for every procedure in the series and that no two consecutive procedures in the series may be more than eight weeks apart; where the gap exceeds eight weeks, the series is treated as having ended and a fresh assessment is required.

Directorate Notice 2026/07, issued on 22 June and effective for procedures performed on or after 1 July 2026, amends section 4 by replacing "thirty days" with "forty-five days" for patients graded ASA I or ASA II at their most recent assessment. The notice leaves the thirty-day window in place for ASA III and above. It also states that where the notice and any earlier local guidance disagree, the notice prevails, but that nothing in the notice alters section 4.3 or section 9.

A separate paragraph of the standard, section 5, governs sedation in the endoscopy suite. Endoscopy patients receiving conscious sedation without an anaesthetist must have a nurse-led fitness check within fourteen days of the procedure, and a check older than fourteen days invalidates the booking. The endoscopy suite runs its own list and its own booking screen, and its fourteen-day rule has been in force unchanged since 2021.

The case concerns Mrs Ondine Ferrall, listed for laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia on Thursday 3 September in Theatre 2, Halvering site, under Mr Pell (surgeon) with Dr Aoki as anaesthetist. Her notes show a single previous procedure at this hospital, an unrelated day-case arthroscopy in 2024 with a different anaesthetist. She has no staged series and no named consultant anaesthetist relationship.

Her pre-operative anaesthetic assessment took place on Monday 27 July 2026 at the Cotterell site. The assessment record grades her ASA II (well-controlled hypertension), with airway and bloods unremarkable and no further investigations requested. The assessment nurse noted that the patient also has a diagnostic gastroscopy pending in the endoscopy suite, which the patient mentioned; that gastroscopy has not yet been booked and forms no part of the 3 September list.

The list coordinator counted the days from 27 July to 3 September and flagged the booking to the directorate because, on her reading, the booking system's thirty-day check had been bypassed when the list was built on 25 June, before the software update that implemented the notice. She asks whether the procedure may proceed on 3 September without a further assessment.

question.instructions: Decide whether Mrs Ferrall's cholecystectomy may proceed on 3 September without a further pre-operative anaesthetic assessment, applying the policy as it stands on that date.

criteria.true: The procedure may proceed on 3 September without a further assessment.
criteria.false: A further assessment is required before the procedure may proceed on 3 September.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: The assessment was on 27 July and surgery is on 3 September, 38 days later. Notice 2026/07 extends the window to forty-five days for ASA I–II patients for procedures performed on or after 1 July, and Mrs Ferrall is graded ASA II with surgery on 3 September, so 38 days is inside the window. Section 4.3 and the eight-week series rule do not apply because she has no series; the endoscopy fourteen-day rule concerns a different list and a pending gastroscopy that is not being performed. That the list was built before the software update does not change which rule governs a procedure performed in September.
provenance.why_hard: The day count exceeds the original thirty-day rule and several clauses (series rule, endoscopy rule, software timing) invite the wrong conclusion.

Report of the Registrar's casework panel, Marrowfield University, on a withdrawal request received in the Fall term.

The Withdrawal and Refund Regulations set out three windows. A student who withdraws from a module on or before the last day of week 8 receives a grade of W on the transcript and a refund of fifty per cent of the module fee. A student who withdraws in weeks 9 to 12 receives a W with no refund. After the end of week 12 no withdrawal is possible and the module is graded on the work submitted, which for a student who stops attending is normally an F. The regulations describe W as a neutral notation that does not count toward the grade-point average.

Regulation 6 provides an exception for medical withdrawal. Where the student is prevented from continuing by their own documented illness or injury, the Registrar may approve a W at any point in the term with a pro-rata refund calculated from the date of the medical certificate. The regulation says explicitly that it covers the student's own health; caring responsibilities for a relative are handled under a separate hardship fund which does not affect the transcript notation or the fee.

An amendment agreed by Senate in June and applying to modules that start in the Fall term or later shortens the refund window: the fifty per cent refund is now available only for withdrawals on or before the last day of week 6. The amendment leaves the W notation unchanged for withdrawals up to the end of week 12 and does not alter Regulation 6. The amendment notes that where the older regulations and the amendment conflict, the amendment applies to Fall-start modules.

Regulation 2, definitions, states that "week 1" begins on the first scheduled day of instruction for the module and each subsequent week runs for seven calendar days from that day. The registration period, which opens before instruction starts, is not counted. The definitions section adds that a request is treated as made on the day the online form is submitted, not on the day a student first raises the matter with an adviser.

Regulation 11, for completeness, deals with students who change a module from audit to credit or credit to audit. Such a change is allowed up to the end of week 4 without penalty and carries no fee adjustment, and after week 4 the module is treated as a withdrawal from the original registration followed by a new registration.

The student, Tobias Renquist, is registered for ECON 2140, a Fall-start module. Registration for the term opened on Monday 17 August. Instruction for ECON 2140 began on Monday 31 August. Mr Renquist first spoke to his academic adviser on 2 October about withdrawing, after his mother was admitted to hospital, and the adviser told him to think it over. He submitted the online withdrawal form on Tuesday 13 October. Attached to the form was a hospital letter concerning his mother's admission and a note from his adviser supporting a hardship-fund application.

Mr Renquist's own health is not in issue and he attended classes until the day he submitted the form. He asks what notation and refund will result.

question.instructions: Determine the transcript and fee outcome of Mr Renquist's withdrawal request under the regulations as they apply to this module.

criteria.w_with_refund: W notation with a fifty per cent fee refund.
criteria.w_no_refund: W notation with no fee refund.
criteria.f_grade: No withdrawal; the module is graded and the outcome is an F.
criteria.medical_withdrawal_prorata: Medical withdrawal under Regulation 6 with a pro-rata refund.
criteria.audit_conversion: The registration is converted to audit under Regulation 11 with no fee adjustment.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: Week 1 began on 31 August (first day of instruction, not the 17 August registration opening). 13 October is day 44 of instruction, which falls in week 7 (days 43–49). Under the Fall amendment the refund window closes at the end of week 6, so the W carries no refund. Regulation 6 does not apply because the illness is his mother's, not his own. Counting from registration would put the request in week 9, which gives the same notation but for the wrong reason; counting from instruction under the unamended rule would wrongly grant the refund.
provenance.why_hard: The correct week depends on the definitions clause and the amended refund window, and the medical letter invites a Regulation 6 reading that the definitions exclude.

Planning desk note, Borough of Ashcombe, concerning an enquiry about a boundary fence at 14 Larkspur Close.

The Residential Boundary Structures Bylaw sets the permit thresholds. A fence in a rear yard may be built without a permit up to a height of 1.8 metres measured from finished grade on the higher side. A fence in a front yard may be built without a permit only up to 1.2 metres. Anything taller than the applicable threshold requires a minor works permit, which carries a fee and a fourteen-day neighbour notification. The bylaw applies to timber, metal and composite fences alike.

Section 3.4 deals with corner lots. Where a lot has frontage on two streets, the yard along each street frontage is treated as a front yard for the purposes of the bylaw, regardless of where the dwelling's front door faces. The section explains that this is to preserve sight lines at intersections and that the treatment cannot be varied by the homeowner's choice of address.

Amendment 2025-11, in force since 1 February 2026, raises the rear-yard threshold to 2.0 metres for lots whose rear boundary abuts a road listed in Schedule 3 as an arterial road, on the ground that traffic noise justifies a taller screen. The amendment does not alter the front-yard threshold and states that it operates subject to section 3.4. Schedule 3 currently lists Willowmere Road, Coppice Lane and the A-classified section of Station Road.

Section 2, definitions, states that "front yard" means the area between a street boundary of the lot and the nearest wall of the dwelling, and "rear yard" means the area between the boundary opposite the principal frontage and the rear wall. Where section 3.4 applies, both street-facing yards are front yards and the remaining yards are side or rear yards.

Section 5 covers retaining walls, which are treated separately from fences. A retaining wall over 1.0 metre in retained height requires an engineer's certificate whether or not a permit is needed for any fence on top of it. Section 5 does not apply to free-standing fences on level ground.

The enquiry is from the owner of 14 Larkspur Close, Mr Ibrahim Solano. The lot is at the junction of Larkspur Close and Willowmere Road. The house's front door and postal frontage face Larkspur Close. The garden on the Willowmere Road side is level and currently has a low hedge; the ground is flat and there is no retaining structure.

Mr Solano proposes a 1.9-metre close-boarded timber fence along the Willowmere Road boundary to reduce traffic noise. He notes that Willowmere Road is on the arterial schedule and that the garden on that side is what he and his neighbours have always called the back garden, since the house faces the close. He has not spoken to the neighbour on the other side.

He asks whether he can put the fence up without a permit.

question.instructions: Decide whether the proposed 1.9-metre fence along the Willowmere Road boundary may be built without a minor works permit.

criteria.true: The fence may be built without a permit.
criteria.false: A minor works permit is required for the fence.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: The lot is a corner lot with frontage on Larkspur Close and Willowmere Road, so under section 3.4 the yard along Willowmere Road is a front yard whatever the owner calls it. The front-yard threshold is 1.2 metres and a 1.9-metre fence exceeds it. Amendment 2025-11 raises only the rear-yard threshold and expressly operates subject to section 3.4, so the arterial listing of Willowmere Road does not help. Section 5 on retaining walls is irrelevant on level ground.
provenance.why_hard: The arterial-road amendment reads as if written for exactly this case, and the corner-lot clause that defeats it sits in a different paragraph.

Customer relations case summary, Corvane Airways, prepared for the compensation review team.

Under the Corvane Passenger Charter, part D, a passenger whose flight arrives at the final destination three hours or more after the scheduled arrival time is entitled to fixed compensation. The amount is set by distance band: 250 credits for journeys of 1,500 kilometres or less and 400 credits for journeys over 1,500 kilometres. The charter states that the compensation is payable in addition to any care provided during the delay and that it is not reduced by meal vouchers or hotel accommodation issued at the airport.

Part D, paragraph 4, removes the entitlement where the delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances, listed as severe weather, air traffic control restrictions, security threats and airport closure. The paragraph adds that crew rostering, aircraft rotation and technical faults discovered in routine maintenance are operational matters and are not extraordinary circumstances.

Charter Bulletin 26-03, effective for journeys commencing on or after 1 March 2026, changes how distance is measured for itineraries booked on a single ticket with a connection. Previously the distances of each flight segment were added together. Under the bulletin, the distance is the great-circle distance between the scheduled origin of the first segment and the scheduled final destination, ignoring the connecting point. The bulletin states that where it conflicts with part D the bulletin governs, and it does not change the three-hour threshold or the amounts.

Part A, definitions, provides that "arrival" means the time at which at least one aircraft door is opened at the gate or stand, not the time of touchdown, and that "scheduled arrival time" is the time shown on the ticket at the time of purchase. Care during the delay is defined separately in part C.

Part E, for completeness, deals with denied boarding. A passenger with a confirmed reservation who is involuntarily denied boarding because the flight is oversold receives 600 credits regardless of distance, together with rebooking. Part E does not apply to passengers who board a delayed flight.

The passenger, Ms Delphine Achterberg, held a single ticket from Rennmark to Sollasvik via the Corvane hub at Ostervale on 9 April 2026. The Rennmark–Ostervale segment is 900 kilometres and the Ostervale–Sollasvik segment is 1,100 kilometres. The great-circle distance from Rennmark direct to Sollasvik, as recorded in the network distance table, is 1,450 kilometres.

The first segment operated on time. The second segment was delayed because the rostered cabin crew had exceeded their permitted duty hours on an earlier rotation and a standby crew had to be called in. At Ostervale Ms Achterberg received a meal voucher. The aircraft touched down at Sollasvik two hours and fifty-five minutes after the scheduled arrival time, and the door opened at the stand three hours and ten minutes after the scheduled arrival time.

The review team must decide what, if anything, she is owed under the charter.

question.instructions: Determine the compensation Ms Achterberg is entitled to under the Corvane Passenger Charter for this journey.

criteria.meal_voucher_only: Only the meal voucher already issued is owed; no credits are payable.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: Arrival is measured at door opening, three hours and ten minutes late, so the three-hour threshold is met. Crew duty-hour rostering is expressly an operational matter, not an extraordinary circumstance. The journey commenced on 9 April 2026, after Bulletin 26-03 took effect, so distance is the great-circle origin-to-destination figure of 1,450 kilometres rather than the summed 2,000 kilometres, which puts it in the 250-credit band. The meal voucher does not reduce the entitlement and part E does not apply.
provenance.why_hard: The touchdown time and the summed segment distance each support a different wrong answer, and the bulletin that changes the distance method sits away from the band table.

Internal review note, Cardholder Disputes, Tallowbridge Bank, on whether a dispute was lodged in time.

The Cardholder Dispute Procedure requires that a dispute over a card transaction be raised within sixty days of the date of the statement on which the transaction first appears. Disputes raised after that window are declined as out of time unless another provision applies, and the customer is told that the bank cannot pursue the merchant. The sixty days are calendar days.

Section 3.2 of the procedure addresses recurring charges, such as subscriptions billed monthly to the card. For a recurring charge the sixty-day window is measured from the most recent charge in the series, not from the first, and a dispute lodged within that window may cover the most recent charge and up to two earlier charges in the same series. The section explains that customers often notice a recurring charge only after several cycles.

Procedure Update 14, applying to disputes received on or after 1 April 2026, changes the starting point for card-not-present transactions. For such transactions the window is measured from the date the transaction posted to the account rather than from the statement date, because online statements are now available daily and the monthly statement date no longer reflects when a customer could have seen the charge. Update 14 states that it does not affect section 3.2, and that where two provisions produce different starting dates for the same dispute, the later of the two starting dates is used.

Section 1, definitions, provides that a dispute is "raised" on the date the bank receives the signed dispute form, whether by post, branch or secure upload. A telephone call or chat conversation in which a customer mentions an intention to dispute does not by itself raise a dispute, though the agent must send the form the same day.

Section 6 is a separate track for transactions the customer says they did not authorise at all. Suspected fraud may be reported within one hundred and twenty days and is investigated by the fraud team, not the disputes team, and section 6 states that it does not apply where the customer acknowledges having set up the relationship with the merchant.

The customer, Mr Evren Castellane, holds a Tallowbridge credit card. He subscribed to an online fitness service in January 2026, paying monthly by card-not-present transaction. He says the service stopped working in April and that he tried to cancel, but the charges continued. The charges posted on 20 January, 20 February, 20 March, 20 April and 20 May; there was no June charge because he cancelled the card's use with the merchant on 2 June. His statements are dated the last day of each month.

He telephoned the bank on 3 July to say he wanted to dispute the charges. The agent sent the form that day. The signed form was received by secure upload on 11 July. He acknowledges that he did set up the subscription himself and is disputing the charges on the basis that the service was not provided from April.

The reviewer must decide whether the dispute was raised in time.

question.instructions: Decide whether Mr Castellane's dispute was raised within the applicable window under the procedure.

criteria.true: The dispute was raised within the applicable window.
criteria.false: The dispute was raised out of time.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: The charges are a recurring series, so under section 3.2 the window runs from the most recent charge, which posted on 20 May. Update 14 applies to card-not-present transactions and measures from the posting date; for the most recent charge that is also 20 May, and even measured from the 31 May statement the later-date rule would only push the start later. The dispute was raised on 11 July when the signed form was received, fifty-two days after 20 May, which is within sixty days. The 3 July call did not raise the dispute but does not matter. Section 6 is excluded because he acknowledges setting up the subscription.
provenance.why_hard: Counting from the January or April charges, or treating the phone call as decisive, produces an out-of-time result, and the recurring-charge clause is easily overlooked.

Circulation supervisor's note, Brackenholt Public Library, on charges for a returned lost item.

The Borrower Charges Schedule provides that an item declared lost is charged at its replacement cost, taken from the catalogue record, plus a processing fee of 8.00 covering re-ordering and cataloguing. The declaration is made either by the borrower or automatically when an item is forty-two days overdue. Overdue fines accrue at 0.20 per day from the due date until the item is declared lost, and the schedule caps the overdue fine on any single item at 10.00.

Paragraph 5 of the schedule deals with lost items that turn up. If the item is returned in good condition within thirty days of the lost declaration, the replacement cost and the processing fee are both cancelled and the borrower pays only the capped overdue fine. If the item is returned more than thirty days after the declaration, the replacement cost is refunded on return but the processing fee stands, because by then the library has normally re-ordered, and the capped overdue fine also stands.

By decision of the Library Board in March, effective from 1 April 2026, the processing fee is abolished for children's borrowers. The board minute records that the change applies to all charges raised on or after that date, that it does not alter the replacement cost or overdue fines, and that in any conflict between the minute and the older schedule the minute prevails.

Paragraph 2, definitions, states that a "children's borrower" is a person holding a card of type J, issued to those under sixteen. The definition turns on the card type, not on the collection the item came from; an adult who borrows a picture book on a type A card is not a children's borrower, and a child who borrows an adult novel on a type J card is.

Paragraph 9 covers items obtained through inter-library loan from another authority. Lost inter-library items are charged at whatever the lending authority invoices, which may exceed the catalogue replacement cost, and the processing fee for such items is 15.00 rather than 8.00. Paragraph 9 applies only to items whose barcode begins with ILL.

The item is a hardback picture book from the children's collection, barcode 3120067741, replacement cost 14.99. It was borrowed on a type A card held by Ms Priya Vandersloot, who took it out for her daughter. The item became forty-two days overdue and was automatically declared lost on 12 May 2026; overdue fines had accrued from the due date, and the system shows the capped amount.

Ms Vandersloot returned the book, undamaged, on 16 June 2026. The desk assistant noted that the book had been re-ordered on 20 May and the replacement copy is on the shelf. Ms Vandersloot says her daughter, who is nine, is the real borrower and that the fee should not apply to a children's book.

The supervisor must decide what Ms Vandersloot owes.

question.instructions: Determine the total charge Ms Vandersloot owes for the returned item under the schedule and the board decision.

criteria.capped_fine_only: Only the capped overdue fine of 10.00.
criteria.processing_fee_and_capped_fine: The processing fee of 8.00 plus the capped overdue fine of 10.00.
criteria.replacement_and_processing: The replacement cost of 14.99 plus the processing fee and the capped fine.
criteria.lender_rate: The lending authority's invoice plus the 15.00 inter-library processing fee.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: The item was returned on 16 June, thirty-five days after the 12 May lost declaration, so under paragraph 5 the replacement cost is refunded but the processing fee and the capped overdue fine stand. The board's abolition of the processing fee applies to children's borrowers defined by card type J; the card is type A, so the fee remains despite the item being a children's book and the daughter being the reader. The barcode does not begin with ILL, so paragraph 9 is irrelevant.
provenance.why_hard: The thirty-day boundary and the card-type definition each sit apart from the clause a reader would apply, and the 'children's book' argument sounds right.

Outpatient access team note, Winterlow Hospitals Trust, on a proposed discharge back to the GP for non-attendance.

The Outpatient Access Policy states that a patient who does not attend two appointments in the same specialty within any rolling twelve-month period is discharged from the clinic and returned to the care of their GP, with a letter explaining that a new referral is needed. The policy describes this as necessary to protect clinic capacity and says the count is made by the booking team at the point of the second non-attendance.

Section 7 exempts patients who are on the trust's safeguarding register, patients under eighteen, and patients whose appointment was arranged by the trust's own transport service and where the transport did not arrive. For those patients a non-attendance is recorded but is never counted toward discharge, and the clinic offers a further appointment.

Access Policy Amendment 3, effective 1 January 2026, adds that a non-attendance counts toward discharge only if the appointment reminder was sent to the patient's recorded contact details at least five days before the appointment date. The amendment explains that reminders sent late were found to be the main cause of avoidable non-attendance. It states that it applies to any non-attendance occurring on or after its effective date and that it does not remove the section 7 exemptions.

Section 2, definitions, provides that "did not attend" means the patient neither attended nor cancelled before the scheduled start time of the clinic session. A cancellation received by telephone or through the patient portal before the session starts, however late, is recorded as a patient cancellation and is not a non-attendance, though three patient cancellations within six months trigger a separate review by the clinic manager which does not lead to discharge.

Section 9 deals with patients who arrive late. A patient who arrives after their appointment time but before the end of the session is seen if the clinician agrees and otherwise rebooked; late arrival is recorded as attendance for the purposes of this policy.

The patient is Mr Kasimir Oyelowo, aged forty-four, under the rheumatology clinic. He is not on the safeguarding register and has never used trust transport. His record shows three entries in the past twelve months. On 3 February 2026 he did not attend and did not cancel; the reminder for that appointment was sent by text on 28 January. On 14 June 2026 he did not attend and did not cancel; the reminder was sent by text on 11 June, because the appointment had been brought forward at short notice when a slot became free. On 2 September 2026 the clinic session started at 09:00; the portal log shows a cancellation submitted by the patient at 08:50 that morning, and the reminder for that appointment had been sent on 21 August.

The booking team has flagged the record for discharge on the basis that this is the third time in twelve months that Mr Oyelowo has not been seen. The access team must decide whether discharge under the policy is correct.

question.instructions: Decide whether Mr Oyelowo should be discharged to his GP under the Outpatient Access Policy.

criteria.true: Discharge under the policy is correct.
criteria.false: Discharge under the policy is not correct.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: Only the 3 February entry is a countable non-attendance: its reminder was sent six days before. The 14 June non-attendance does not count under Amendment 3 because the reminder was sent three days before the appointment. The 2 September entry is a patient cancellation under section 2 because it was submitted before the 09:00 session start, so it is not a non-attendance at all. One countable non-attendance does not meet the two-in-twelve-months threshold, so discharge is wrong. Section 7 exemptions are not engaged.
provenance.why_hard: The record shows three missed contacts, and each of the two that do not count is excluded by a different clause in a different paragraph.

Examinations office file note, Dunmoor University, on a missed examination and the resulting assessment outcome.

Under the Assessment Regulations, part F, a student who misses a scheduled examination and has approved mitigating circumstances is offered a deferred sitting at the next examination period, marked as a first attempt with no cap. A student who misses an examination without approved mitigating circumstances is recorded as a non-submission and is offered a single resit, with the module mark capped at the pass mark of 40.

Part F, paragraph 3, provides that an application for mitigating circumstances submitted more than five working days after the examination date is treated as if no circumstances had been claimed, whatever its merits, unless the student was hospitalised throughout the period. The paragraph explains that late applications cannot be verified against the examination record in time for the board.

Regulation Change 2026-A, applying to all assessments taking place in the calendar year 2026 and later, replaces "five working days" in paragraph 3 with "ten working days" following a review of student support. The change states that it does not alter the definition of working days and that in any inconsistency between the change and part F the change prevails.

Part A, definitions, provides that "working days" are Monday to Friday excluding the university closure days published in the academic calendar. The academic calendar for 2026 lists the following closure days in the relevant period: Tuesday 2 June to Friday 5 June inclusive (staff development week), together with the usual public holidays, none of which fall in June. The definitions add that an application is submitted on the day it is received by the online portal.

Part G, for completeness, governs coursework extensions. A student may apply for an extension of up to seven days on any coursework deadline before the deadline passes; extensions are not available for examinations, and a coursework extension does not affect an examination outcome on the same module.

The student, Ms Halcyon Mbeki-Ruiz, was scheduled to sit the MATH 2205 examination on Friday 29 May 2026. She did not attend. Her portal application for mitigating circumstances, with a medical certificate covering the examination date, was received on Thursday 18 June 2026. She was not hospitalised. The certificate is accepted on its merits by the panel and the only question is whether the application was in time.

The module leader has noted that he also granted Ms Mbeki-Ruiz a seven-day extension on the MATH 2205 coursework component in April, which she used, and asks whether that has any bearing. The examinations officer must determine the assessment outcome.

question.instructions: Determine the assessment outcome for Ms Mbeki-Ruiz on MATH 2205 under the regulations as they apply in 2026.

criteria.fail_no_resit: The module is failed with no further attempt.
criteria.resit_capped: A single resit with the mark capped at 40.
criteria.deferred_exam: A deferred sitting as a first attempt, uncapped.
criteria.resit_uncapped: A resit as a second attempt without a cap.
criteria.extension_7_days: A seven-day extension under part G.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-shadow-2b
provenance.rationale: The examination was on Friday 29 May 2026, so Change 2026-A applies and the window is ten working days. Counting working days after 29 May and excluding the 2–5 June closure: Monday 1 June is day 1, then 8–12 June are days 2–6, and 15–18 June are days 7–10, so 18 June is the tenth working day and the application is in time. With circumstances approved, part F gives a deferred uncapped sitting. Counting without the closure days would make 18 June the fourteenth working day and wrongly produce a capped resit; the coursework extension is irrelevant to examinations.
provenance.why_hard: The application looks late under both the old five-day rule and a naive ten-day count, and the closure days that make it timely are listed in the definitions paragraph.

Parking services memo, Kettlesby District Council, on a residents' permit application for 27 Fennimore Street.

The Residents' Parking Scheme rules provide that a residents' permit is issued only for a vehicle registered at the applicant's address on the national vehicle register, and the applicant must show the registration document together with proof of residence. The rules state that permits are specific to the vehicle and the zone and cannot be transferred.

Rule 4 provides an exception for company vehicles. Where the vehicle is registered to an employer rather than to the applicant, a permit may be issued on production of a letter on the employer's headed paper confirming that the applicant is the vehicle's sole regular keeper and that it is kept overnight at the applicant's address. The letter must be dated within the last three months.

Scheme Amendment 2026/1, effective 6 April 2026, limits each household to a maximum of two residents' permits in force at any one time. A third application from the same household is refused, and the rules say that the applicant may instead purchase visitor scratch-cards. The amendment states that it applies to applications received on or after its effective date and that existing third permits run to expiry without renewal.

Rule 1, definitions, states that "household" means a single dwelling unit as recorded in the council tax register. Where a property contains a registered secondary suite with its own council tax entry, the suite is a separate household and is counted separately for permit purposes, even though it shares a street address and postcode with the main dwelling. The definitions also provide that "in force" means issued and not expired, surrendered or cancelled.

Rule 8 covers visitor scratch-cards. Each household may buy up to twenty cards a quarter; cards are not valid for the household's own vehicles, and a card displayed in a vehicle that also holds a residents' permit is treated as misuse and may lead to cancellation of the permit.

The property at 27 Fennimore Street contains a main house and a basement flat. The basement flat has been on the council tax register as a separate entry, 27A Fennimore Street, since 2019. The main house currently holds two residents' permits in force, one for each of the owners' cars, both issued in 2025 and expiring in 2027.

The applicant, Ms Rosalind Achebe-Tran, is the tenant of the basement flat and has lived there since March 2026. Arboricultural officer's note, Greyhaven Borough, on a resident's question about removing a garden tree.

The Tree Protection Bylaw provides that a tree with a trunk diameter of 30 centimetres or more on private land within the borough may not be removed without a tree removal permit. A permit, where granted, is conditional on replacement planting of one nursery-standard tree for each tree removed, and the bylaw provides that removal without a permit is an offence carrying a fine. Trees below the threshold may be removed without any permit or notification.

Section 6 provides an exception for dead, dying or dangerous trees. Such a tree may be removed without a permit, but the owner must notify the borough within five working days of removal and must supply a report from a qualified arborist confirming the tree's condition. No replacement planting is required under section 6.

Bylaw Amendment 4, in force from 1 January 2026, changes the point at which trunk diameter is measured from 1.0 metre above ground level to 1.4 metres above ground level, bringing the borough into line with the standard forestry measurement. The amendment states that it applies to any removal on or after its effective date and that in any inconsistency with the original bylaw the amendment prevails. The threshold figure of 30 centimetres is unchanged.

Section 1, definitions, provides that "dangerous" means that the tree, or a substantial part of it, is likely to fall and cause injury or damage, as confirmed in writing by a qualified arborist; the owner's own opinion, or a neighbour's, is not sufficient. The definitions also provide that "trunk diameter" is the diameter of the main stem at the measurement height, and that for a multi-stemmed tree the largest stem is used.

The office's address file shows that 7 Kiln Lane was recorded as outside the parish on the boundary map of 2010.
